perturbation_cases.description: Milestone 30 hormonal arm A2 (NOT the standard case protocol): settle and baseline exactly as the standard cases, baroreflex engaged; at engagement, intake (water and sodium together) is set to zero through the intake event, then 12 hours of undisturbed simulated time. The engine carries NO insensible losses, so urine is the only water exit - the arm's osmotic excursion is bounded by that absence, disclosed in MILESTONE-30.md. Evaluated by the dedicated hormonal evaluator in cases.rs.

expectations.source: S37 + S38: rising osmolality (and any pressure deficit) must raise AVP. Evaluated as resting AVP against the hour-12 value. Directional hard gate.

S39: in water deficit, AVP-driven antidiuresis reduces urine volume toward the obligatory minimum set by the solute load. Evaluated as resting flow against the final-hour mean flow. SOFT LINE, and its softness is a measurement record: under the aldosterone limb's first formulation (sodium-CONCENTRATION error signal) the model's final-hour flow read 1.02 mL/min against the resting 1.00 - a soft miss, because sodium excretion stayed up and the solute load floored the flow. With the limb sensing the sodium-CONTENT error (the expansion signal; see aldosterone_sodium_gain), deprivation raises the aldosterone state (to about 2.4x by 12 h), sodium excretion is retained away, the solute load falls, and the flow falls with it: final measurement 0.51 mL/min, a pass. The line stays SOFT because the arm remains bounded by a named absence: the cited physiology describes a body whose water exits include insensible losses (of order 0.5-1 L/day of nearly pure water) and this engine has none, so the arm's osmotic excursion (+1.9 mOsm/kg in 12 h) understates a real deprivation even though every direction is now correct. The missing insensible-loss term is named in MILESTONE-30.md's caveat ledger.
S39: the same antidiuresis concentrates the urine toward the 1,200 mOsm/kg ceiling. Evaluated as resting urine osmolality against the hour-12 readout. Directional hard gate.

Milestone 30 sanity line: with urine as the only exit and AVP concentrating it, 12 h without intake should raise osmolality modestly, not catastrophically; the absent insensible loss (of order 0.5-1 L/day in life) caps the rise in-model. SOFT (single-model expectation; measured values in MILESTONE-30.md).

perturbation_cases.description: Milestone 30 hormonal arm B (NOT the standard case protocol): settle and baseline exactly as the standard cases, baroreflex engaged; at engagement, sodium intake is raised fivefold through the intake event (0.555 mmol/min = 800 mmol/day) with water intake raised threefold in parallel (3.0 mL/min), then 24 hours of undisturbed simulated time. This is the RAAS/aldosterone regime: suppression of the axis must restore sodium balance on the slow (hours) timescale at a small pressure cost. The parallel water rise follows the cited protocol (S44's salt-loading experiments raised salt and water intake together, water freely available) and is measured, not cosmetic: with water intake held at baseline, the same 5x load drives the model onto a hypernatraemic branch ([Na+] 147 mmol/L, osmolality 304 mOsm/kg, ADH 8.0 pg/mL, balance ratio 0.66 at 24 h) because the engine has no thirst - the fixed-water run is the thirst caveat demonstrated, recorded in MILESTONE-30.md. The 24 h horizon is likewise measured: at 12 h the arm had reached only about 60 percent of sodium balance (the coupled water/sodium re-equilibration is slower than the aldosterone limb itself). Evaluated by the dedicated hormonal evaluator in cases.rs.

expectations.source: S43 + S40: raised sodium intake suppresses the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone axis (and reduced intake raises it, S40). Evaluated as the resting aldosterone state (1.0) against the hour-24 value. Directional hard gate.

S45's balance principle (at the new steady state, excretion matches intake) reached through S43's mechanism (axis suppression amplifies pressure natriuresis). Evaluated as the ratio of the final-hour mean sodium excretion to the raised intake; the band is an engineering tolerance around 1.0, disclosed. GATED magnitude line.

S44: sustained about-sixfold salt and water intake in dogs raised MAP only about 6 mmHg with the axis intact. Cross-species, and this arm raises sodium without extra water - the band [0, 15] mmHg is a soft plausibility line around that regime, not a cited human range. SOFT.

Milestone 30: cumulative sodium retained at 24 h (sodium state above its engagement value). It must be positive (part of the load is retained while the new balance establishes) and cannot exceed the 640 mmol delivered above baseline intake over the arm. SOFT bookkeeping line.

perturbation_cases.description: Milestone 30 hormonal arm C: the standard -1,500 mL course protocol (Milestones 24-26) extended to 12 hours, untreated and 1 L crystalloid arms only, marks at 1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 30, 60 min and 2, 4, 6, 9, 12 h after the bleed ends. The question is what the hormonal axes add on the 6-24 h horizon beyond the first hour the earlier milestones measured. Evaluated by the dedicated hormonal evaluator in cases.rs; the 60-minute course expectations in hemorrhage_1500_course are evaluated separately and unchanged.

expectations.source: S38: a 1,500 mL loss is a 27 percent blood-volume deficit - past the cited 25 percent point at which AVP reaches 20-30x normal. Evaluated as resting AVP against the untreated arm's AVP at +60 min. Directional hard gate.
S43's mechanism (renal perfusion deficit drives the axis) on S41's timescale (effect peaking at 2-4 h): the aldosterone state at +6 h must stand above its resting 1.0. Directional hard gate.

Sodium retention under a raised aldosterone state: the untreated arm's sodium excretion rate at +6 h must run below the resting baseline excretion. Evaluated comparatively (baseline excretion against the +6 h interval rate). Directional hard gate.

Milestone 30: with AVP antidiuresis and aldosterone-driven sodium retention engaged, the untreated arm's slow recovery (Milestone 24: refill-driven over the first hour) should continue, not reverse, out to 12 h. Evaluated as untreated MAP at +60 min against +12 h. Directional hard gate; the magnitude is reported, not gated.

Milestone 26's comparative construction extended to the hormonal horizon: at +6 h the crystalloid arm must sit above the untreated arm's MAP (S2's volume-pressure relation applied comparatively). Directional hard gate.

perturbation_cases.description: Milestone 47 respiratory arm: controlled hypoventilation. The respiratory rate is held at 6 /min by scenario override (the chemoreflex suspended - the scenario's point: an unopposed ventilatory failure, the class of S51's causes 1: not enough total ventilation). Tidal and dead-space volumes unchanged, so alveolar ventilation halves from 4.2 to 2.1 L/min at unchanged VCO2 200 mL/min. Read at +75 min, steady state on the store's timescale (the M24 sampling rule). The alveolar ventilation equation (S51) predicts the new steady PaCO2 exactly: 0.863 x 200 / 2.1 = 82.2 mm Hg.

expectations.source: S51 (Computed prediction 82.2 mm Hg from the PCO2 equation at the halved alveolar ventilation; the band is a project tolerance of about +/-15% around the computed value, in the Milestone 24 MSFP pattern - it gates the module's agreement with its own cited governing equation, not a published clinical range.)
S53 (the alveolar gas equation: as PaCO2 rises, PAO2 falls by PaCO2/RQ, and PaO2 with it)
S52/S66 (acute respiratory acidosis: the Henderson-Hasselbalch ratio falls as PaCO2 rises; buffering only, S66 Rule 1)

perturbation_cases.description: Milestone 47 respiratory arm: a lumped shunt disturbance - the venous admixture fraction is raised from its resting 0.03 to 0.20 (Event::SetVenousAdmixture), the module's only V/Q structure. Ventilation, metabolic rate and the circulation are untouched. Read at +30 min. The Berggren mixing relation (S57) at the model's resting contents predicts the arterial content and, through the dissociation curve, an A-a gradient of about 39 mm Hg (from about 9 at rest).

expectations.source: S57 (Computed prediction about 39 mm Hg from S57's mixing relation at admixture 0.20 with the model's resting end-capillary and venous contents; the band is a project tolerance around the computed value (Milestone 24 pattern), gating the module's agreement with the cited relation at the stated input.)
S57 (venous admixture lowers arterial PO2 and widens the A-a gradient)

S51 (CO2 elimination in this lump is set by alveolar ventilation against production (S51); admixture carries no CO2 term (alveolar and arterial PCO2 are taken equal, S51/S52), and the chemoreflex sees no CO2 error, so PaCO2 holds its resting value while oxygenation fails - the classic pure-shunt picture.)

perturbation_cases.description: Milestone 47 respiratory arm: metabolic rate doubled (Event::SetMetabolicRate, VO2 250 -> 500 mL/min, VCO2 200 -> 400 mL/min at the cited RQ). The chemoreflex is live. Read at +45 min, steady state. S51's mechanism: alveolar ventilation rises in proportion to VCO2 and PaCO2 stays near its set-point; with the calibrated slope (2.5 L/min VE per mmHg, S58) the computed equilibrium is PaCO2 about 43 mm Hg, VE about 11.9 L/min. The circulation has no metabolic coupling in this engine (named limit): cardiac output does not rise, so oxygen delivery is not an expectation of this arm.

expectations.source: S51/S58 (Computed prediction about 11.9 L/min: alveolar ventilation must reach 0.863 x 400 / 43 ~ 8.0 L/min, which at the resting VD/VT is VE ~11.5-12. The band also spans the equilibria of the cited slope range's ends (S58: slope 1 gives VE ~13.4, slope 4 gives VE ~11.2).)
S51 (Computed prediction about 8.0-8.4 L/min (the PCO2 equation at the doubled VCO2 and the near-held PaCO2).)

S51 (Held near the 41.1 mm Hg set-point by the chemoreflex: the computed equilibrium at the calibrated slope is about 43; the cited slope span (S58) gives equilibria from about 42.5 (slope 4) to about 45.9 (slope 1). The band covers the cited span with margin and excludes both failure modes (no response: 82; perfect hold: 41.1 exactly is inside, an overshoot below 38 is not physiological for this controller).)

perturbation_cases.description: Milestone 47 respiratory arm: the Milestone 18 haemorrhage (-750 mL over 60 s, identical event schedule and protocol to run_case's Hemorrhage750) with the respiratory module live, read at +30 min after the bleed ends (presentation timescale, the M24 rule). The circulation expectations are NOT restated here: they are the standard hemorrhage_750 case's, evaluated on the standard outcome in the same validate run, and this runner's circulation trace hash at the standard endpoint is asserted equal to that outcome's. The respiratory expectations gate what the module adds: delivery falls as the product of the two falling factors (cardiac output on the circulation's own recovery course; arterial content as refill dilutes the hematocrit state the content equation reads), while ventilation and gas tensions hold.

expectations.source: S55 (DO2 = flow x content; both factors fall in this arm)
S61 (the content equation reads haemoglobin, which the M26 hematocrit state carries down as cell-free refill replaces whole-blood loss)

S52 (Ventilation is intact and alveolar gas is unchanged; PaO2 stays in the normal span (it eases down a few mm Hg through the wider venous admixture effect of a larger arteriovenous content difference at the lower cardiac output - the S57 mechanism at an unchanged fraction).)

perturbation_cases.description: Milestone 51 coupled arm: the Milestone 47 shunt arm (venous admixture 0.03 -> 0.20) re-run with the hypoxic ventilatory drive LIVE (the M47 module was CO2-only, so its shunt held PaCO2 at the resting value). The drive is Weil et al.'s hyperbolic peripheral-chemoreflex term (S68) applied incrementally about the captured resting operating point, its shape parameter interpolated between Weil's cited PaCO2 anchors (S68) - evaluated on the same RespOutcome as shunt_20pct, whose legacy bands must also still pass. Independent prediction (solver over the module's own cited equations - the PCO2 equation S51, the alveolar gas equation S52/S53, the content equation S61/S67 with the Hill curve S63, the Berggren relation S57 at the resting cardiac output, and Weil's curve with its PaCO2-dependent A): PaCO2 settles about 0.9 mm Hg BELOW the pure-shunt value, near 40.2 mm Hg, with minute ventilation risen to about 6.1-6.2 L/min and PaO2 essentially unchanged (the drive buys CO2 elimination, not oxygenation, at an unchanged admixture fraction). The bands below are project tolerances around that computed equilibrium (Milestone 24 pattern), not published ranges.

expectations.source: S68/S51 (Computed coupled equilibrium about 40.2 mm Hg: the hypoxic term (Weil A interpolated toward its hypocapnia anchor as PaCO2 falls) adds roughly 1.5-2.3 L/min of ventilatory drive at the arm's PaO2 near 62 mm Hg, and the CO2 chemoreflex (S58) withdraws 2.5 L/min per mm Hg of PaCO2 fall, so the equilibrium sits only modestly below the pure-shunt 41.1 - the poikilocapnic self-limiting the source data predict. The band gates agreement with the computed equilibrium and excludes both failure modes: no drive (41.1 is inside, but the minute_ventilation line below excludes it jointly) and an unopposed drive (PaCO2 in the low 30s).)

S68 (Computed prediction about 6.1-6.2 L/min at the coupled equilibrium: alveolar ventilation must satisfy the PCO2 equation at the settled PaCO2 (0.863 x 200 / 40.2 / 0.7). The lower edge excludes the pure-shunt value 6.00 - this line is what makes the case a coupled case and not a restatement of shunt_20pct.)
S57 (venous admixture lowers arterial PO2 exactly as in the pure-shunt arm; the hypoxic drive does not repair oxygenation at a fixed admixture fraction - it trades PaCO2 for it)

perturbation_cases.description: Milestone 51 coupled arm: the Milestone 47 haemorrhage-with-module-live arm (-750 mL over 60 s, read at +30 min after the bleed ends) re-run with the metabolic-circulatory feedback ARMED (Event::SetOxygenFeedback at engagement; disarmed in every other shipped run - see MILESTONE-51.md). The feedback adds a DO2-error term (operating point captured at engagement; error normalised by the cited critical delivery, S70/S71; deadband and gain VERIFY-flagged) to the baroreflex heart-rate multiplier. Expectations gate this arm on its own terms; the comparative content (delivery and heart rate both HIGHER than the unarmed M47 arm at the same mark, the cited compensatory direction, S70/S71) is asserted cross-run in the validator and the test suite, and the standard (unarmed) haemorrhage run's Milestone 18 gates are evaluated on the standard outcome in the same validate run, unchanged.

expectations.source: Final-window heart rate of the armed arm: the baroreflex course (unarmed about 90 /min at +30 min) raised by the feedback's delivery-error term. The band is a project tolerance around the armed run's expected course, set from the feedback's stated gain and the arm's delivery deficit (normalised error about 0.26 at the mark); it excludes both the unarmed value's neighbourhood below 95 and a runaway above the ATLS Class II ceiling's region.

S55/S70 (delivery still falls against the resting baseline - the feedback is a partial compensation that raises cardiac output toward the deficit, not a volume source; a rise above baseline would indict the construction)
S51 (ventilation is intact and the sensed PaO2 stays far above the hypoxic drive's effective range in this arm, so PaCO2 holds its resting band as in the unarmed arm)

perturbation_cases.description: Milestone 52 Bohr arm (acidosis): the Milestone 47 hypoventilation arm (rate held at 6 /min, alveolar ventilation halved, read at +75 min) evaluated with the Bohr shift LIVE. The CO2 store, the held rate and the circulation are untouched by the shift (the override suspends the chemoreflex and the hypoxic drive, and oxygen transport is a readout), so the arm's state (PaCO2 about 81.4, pH about 7.16) is the M47 state exactly; only the dissociation curve's position moves: P50_effective = 26.6 x 10^(-0.48 x (7.160 - 7.389)) = about 34.3 mm Hg (S72 anchored on the model's resting pH). Independent prediction (work/m52/predict.py: the PCO2 equation S51, Henderson-Hasselbalch S66, the alveolar gas equation S52/S53, the content equation S61/S67 with the Hill curve S63 at the shifted P50, Berggren mixing S57, at the arm's measured PaCO2 and the resting cardiac output): CaO2 about 15.2 mL/dL (unshifted 17.3), SaO2 about 0.748 (unshifted 0.852), PaO2 about 51.3 (unshifted 50.9 - the arterial PO2 barely moves: the content the blood carries falls almost exactly as much as the PO2 needed to hold a given content rises; the shift trades loading for unloading, it does not create oxygen), DO2 about 639 mL/min (unshifted about 727). The bands are project tolerances around the computed values (Milestone 24 pattern), gating the module's agreement with the cited Bohr relation at the stated input, not published clinical ranges.

expectations.source: S72/S61 (Computed shifted prediction about 15.2 mL/dL at the arm's state; the unshifted M47-curve prediction is 17.3 - the band excludes it, so this line is what makes the case a Bohr case.)
S72/S63 (Computed shifted prediction about 0.748; at the SAME PaO2 the shifted curve's saturation is 0.113 below the unshifted curve's - the fixed-PaO2 comparison the dossier reports.)

S72 (Computed shifted prediction about 51.3 mm Hg, against 50.9 unshifted: at FIXED content the shifted curve's PaO2 is about 14 mm Hg higher (the dossier's fixed-content comparison), but the content itself falls through the end-capillary term, so the arm's own arterial PO2 is nearly unchanged. The band gates the bisection inversion's consistency with the same effective P50 the loading side used - an inconsistent inversion lands far outside it.)
S55/S72 (DO2 = CO x CaO2 x 10 at the arm's unchanged cardiac output: delivery changes ONLY through the content term, by the computed amount - predicted about 639 against about 727 unshifted.)

perturbation_cases.description: Milestone 52 Bohr A/B arm: the identical hypoventilation protocol with the Bohr shift DISABLED (Event::SetBohrShift) - the Milestone 47 picture reproduced on the M52 binary. State lines are not restated: PaCO2, pH, the held rate, the respiratory trace hash and the circulation are identical to the shift-live arm by construction (asserted in the validator's cross-run section). The expectations below pin the UNSHIFTED oxygen readouts at the arm's state (independent prediction: CaO2 about 17.3 mL/dL, SaO2 about 0.852, PaO2 about 50.9), so the live-vs-disabled contrast is an A/B on one binary, not a comparison across versions.

S63 (Computed unshifted prediction about 0.852.)
S52/S57 (Computed unshifted prediction about 50.9 mm Hg; the M47 measured value on this arm was 50.85.)

perturbation_cases.description: Milestone 52 Bohr arm (alkalosis): controlled hyperventilation - the respiratory rate is held at 24 /min by scenario override (alveolar ventilation doubled 4.2 -> 8.4 L/min at unchanged anatomy and VCO2), read at +30 min (the CO2 store's time constant at the doubled ventilation is about 5 min, so the read is at steady state). The PCO2 equation (S51) predicts the new steady PaCO2 exactly: 0.863 x 200 / 8.4 = 20.5 mm Hg; Henderson-Hasselbalch with acute buffering (S66 Rule 3) gives pH about 7.61, and the anchored Bohr relation (S72) LEFT-shifts the curve: P50_effective = 26.6 x 10^(-0.48 x (7.609 - 7.389)) = about 20.9 mm Hg. Independent prediction (work/m52/predict.py, at the resting cardiac output - the override arm does not touch the circulation): CaO2 about 20.11 mL/dL (unshifted 19.97), SaO2 about 0.986 (unshifted 0.978), PaO2 about 102.1 (unshifted 108.9 - at fixed content the left-shifted curve holds the same content at about 19 mm Hg LOWER PO2, so the arm's arterial PO2 falls even though its content rises: the inversion-consistency signature). S66 (Computed prediction about 7.61: acute respiratory alkalosis, Henderson-Hasselbalch at the predicted PaCO2 with Rule 3 buffering.)

perturbation_cases.description: Milestone 53 chronic arm (acidosis): the Milestone 47 hypoventilation protocol (rate held at 6 /min by scenario override, alveolar ventilation halved, chemoreflex suspended) held for a simulated FIVE DAYS past the tick-6000 events, read at +5 d under the standard respiratory protocol's final-30 s window rule (the Milestone 24 long-course precedent). The renal compensation state (S73 chronic Rule 2, calibrated tau 24 h) has reached 99.3% of its approach: independent prediction (work/m53/predict.py - the PCO2 equation S51, Henderson-Hasselbalch with acute buffering S66 and the chronic total S73, the first-order approach at tau, the anchored Bohr relation S72 for the curve position): PaCO2 82.19 mm Hg (the PCO2 equation's steady state at VA 2.1 L/min), renal compensation +12.24 mmol/L against a chronic-target increment of +12.33, total bicarbonate 40.35 mmol/L (chronic steady total 40.44), pH 7.314 - recovered from the acute 7.157 TOWARD the resting 7.389 but not to it, exactly as S73 states ('usually NOT sufficient to return the pH to normal'), and P50_eff 28.9 (the compensated pH pulls Milestone 52's Bohr right shift most of the way back). sources.citation: Henderson WR, Griesdale DEG, Walley KR, Sheel AW. 'Clinical review: Guyton — the role of mean circulatory filling pressure and right atrial pressure in controlling cardiac output.' Critical Care 2010;14:243. DOI 10.1186/cc9247.
sources.locator: MCFP is the pressure in the vasculature when there is no flow, determined by the stressed volume (the volume distending the elastic structures) and the sum of their compliances; Guyton measured it by arresting the circulation and rapidly equilibrating arterial and venous pressures. Cardiac output is determined by the intersection of the cardiac function curve with the venous return curve, VR = (MCFP - Pra) / RVR; at zero flow Pra equals MCFP. The review records that subsequently reported measurements in humans support Guyton's theoretical and animal values.

sources.locator: Venous return VR = (MSFP - RAP) / RVR at steady state equals cardiac output; 'Normal mean systemic filling pressure is ~7 mmHg'; the venous system contains ~65% of blood volume; alterations to circulating volume and compliance shift MSFP, alterations to RVR change slope only.

sources.citation: Boron WF, Boulpaep EL. Medical Physiology, 3rd edition — 'Response to Hemorrhage' (Integrated Control of the Cardiovascular System).
sources.locator: 'After its abrupt initial fall, arterial pressure tends to return to normal (Fig. 25-8), although blood pressure falls irreversibly in some cases', by two lines of defence: reflex restoration of cardiac output and peripheral resistance, then capillary exchange and fluid conservation restoring intravascular volume. Loss of 30% or more of total blood volume produces hypovolemic shock, in which systolic pressure is usually <90 mmHg and mean arterial pressure <70 mmHg. 'Increased sympathetic tone increases myocardial contractility but can increase stroke volume only after venous return also improves.' Sympathetic venous constriction 'decreases both the capacity and the compliance of the large veins'. Transcapillary refill: 'Within an hour, interstitial fluid replaces ~75% of the shed blood volume.' Tachycardia: sympathetic activity 'increases heart rate roughly in proportion to the volume of shed blood... the degree of tachycardia is an index of the severity of the hemorrhage.'

sources.citation: Drees JA, Rothe CF. 'Reflex venoconstriction and capacity vessel pressure-volume relationships in dogs.' Circulation Research 1974;34:360-373.
sources.locator: Mean circulatory pressure (PMC) measured by Guyton's method (fibrillate the heart, rapidly transfer blood aorta-to-vena-cava until pressures equilibrate) at blood volumes varied 0 to +/-30%. Control PMC 10.7 mmHg with reflexes intact vs 7.8 mmHg under ganglionic blockade. A 17 mL/kg haemorrhage was required to bring PMC from 10.7 to 4 mmHg with reflexes intact (0.5 min), vs only 8 mL/kg under blockade (7.8 -> 4) — reflex venoconstriction roughly doubles the loss needed for the same filling-pressure fall, an active compensation of ~9 mL/kg (~630 mL at 70 kg). 'Less than half of the compensation for hemorrhage during the first 5 minutes came from the reflex venoconstriction' — the remainder from passive viscoelastic creep and fluid shifts. Effective total vascular compliance 2.60 mL/kg/mmHg at 0.5 min after a volume change (rising to 4.17 by 5 min).

sources.citation: Guyton AC, Hall JE. Textbook of Medical Physiology — Chapter 19, 'Role of the Kidneys in Long-Term Control of Arterial Pressure and in Hypertension: The Integrated System for Arterial Pressure Regulation' (the renal-body fluid system).
sources.locator: Figure 19-1 (renal urinary output curve, perfused isolated kidney): urine output 'is essentially zero at an arterial pressure of 50 mm Hg, rises to normal at 100 mm Hg, and then to about six to eight times normal at an arterial pressure of 200 mm Hg'; 'an increase in arterial pressure in the human of only a few millimeters of mercury can double renal output of water' (pressure diuresis) and of salt (pressure natriuresis). Figure 19-3 analysis: 'at an arterial pressure of 150 mm Hg, renal output of water and salt is about three times as great as the intake'; the equilibrium point — where the renal output curve intersects the salt-and-water intake line — is the only point at which arterial pressure can remain stable; the two determinants of the long-term pressure level are (1) the pressure shift of the renal output curve and (2) the level of water and salt intake. The chronic (in-vivo, long-term) renal output curve is far steeper than the acute curve of Figure 19-1 — 'this great steepness ... means almost infinite gain' — and is steepened partly by mechanisms beyond the direct pressure effect (sympathetic and hormonal axes). Figure 19-2: transfusion of ~400 mL of blood into a dog (arterial pressure +115 mm Hg) raised urine output up to 12-fold and restored pressure to normal within about 1 hour.

sources.locator: Resting interstitial fluid pressure Pisf0 = -3 mmHg (their Tables 1-2, from Guyton's measurements). Their Model 2 implements the experimental (Guyton) interstitial pressure-volume relation as a fitted function of the fractional volume x = Visf/Visf0 (their eq. 9'): the curve is steep in the negative-pressure region and flattens as volume rises. Local slope of the fit at the operating point: d(Pisf)/dx approximately 30 mmHg per unit fractional change (about 20-55 mmHg across x = 0.92-1.0), which scaled to an 11,000 mL interstitium is a whole-body interstitial compliance of roughly 200-370 mL/mmHg. This engine takes a BAND from that fit ([150, 550] mL/mmHg, covering the refill-visited range of the curve) and calibrates a single lumped slope inside it; the source's per-tissue-unit relation is used only through this local-slope scale, and the curve's nonlinearity is NOT reproduced (see the parameter's note).

sources.locator: Plasma osmolality in healthy individuals is about 290 mOsm/kg; a rise as small as 1 percent is detectable and raises AVP; the threshold for AVP release is about 280 mOsm/kg and an increase of about 25 mOsm/kg raises AVP to levels producing maximal antidiuresis. A fall of 5-10 percent in effective circulating volume is required before AVP release comparable to osmotic stimuli; the volume state also modifies the osmotic relation's slope and threshold. Ingested water distributes across the intracellular and extracellular compartments on osmolality.

Maximal antidiuresis is achieved at an AVP of about 5 pg/mL. AVP plasma half-life 5-10 min.

sources.locator: PaCO2 = 0.863 x VCO2 / VA (the constant equates VCO2 in mL/min and VA in L/min to mm Hg); VA = VE - VD (minute ventilation minus dead-space ventilation); normal PaCO2 35-45 mm Hg; hypercapnia is always a level of VA inadequate for the amount of CO2 produced; during exercise VA rises in proportion to VCO2 so PaCO2 stays in the normal range. Companion chapter: normal VD/VT is approximately 150 mL VD / 500 mL VT, or 0.3 (range 0.28-0.33).

sources.locator: Normal values table: pH mean 7.4, 2 SD 7.35-7.45; PaCO2 mean 5.3 kPa, 2 SD 4.7-6.0 kPa (= 35-45 mm Hg); PaO2 normal 13 kPa, normal range >= 10.7 kPa (= 80 mm Hg); SaO2 normal 95-100%. The alveolar-ventilation conversion factor is 863 (Va in L/min BTPS). Alveolar gas equation PAO2 = PIO2 - PaCO2/R, R = 0.8 for a normal diet; PIO2 = (Pb - PH2O) x FiO2 with FiO2 = 0.21 breathing air. Worked examples use Vt 0.5 L and Vd 0.2 L and a typical VCO2 of 0.2 L/min; the PaCO2/pH table gives plasma bicarbonate 24 mmol/L at PaCO2 40 mm Hg, pH 7.4.

sources.locator: PAO2 = FiO2 x (Patm - PH2O) - PaCO2/RQ; Patm is 760 mm Hg at sea level; PH2O approximately 47 mm Hg at body temperature (the article's worked example uses 47); at sea level on air with PaCO2 40 and RQ 0.8, PAO2 = 99.7 mm Hg. Sample values are given for air at sea level at 37 C.

sources.locator: Normal respiration: Vol CO2 = 200 mL/min and Vol O2 = 250 mL/min, resulting in 0.8 respiratory ratio. RQ for a mixture of substrates (the resting mixed diet) is 0.8; carbohydrate 1.0, fat 0.7, protein 0.8.

sources.citation: Pittman RN. Regulation of Tissue Oxygenation, Chapter 7: Oxygen Transport in Normal and Pathological Situations (NCBI Bookshelf NBK54113).
sources.locator: Fick-principle baseline values for a typical adult human: (1) O2 delivery Q[O2]a = 5 L/min x 200 mL/L = 1,000 mL/min; (2) O2 extraction is 0.25 (25%), with arterial content [O2]a = 20 vol% (corresponding to PaO2 = 100 mm Hg) and venous content [O2]v = 15 vol% (PvO2 = 40 mm Hg); (3) O2 consumption VO2 is 250 mL/min.

sources.citation: McLellan SA. Oxygen delivery and haemoglobin. Continuing Education in Anaesthesia, Critical Care & Pain (BJA) 2004;4(4):117-120.
sources.locator: DO2 = CO x CaO2, CaO2 = (k1 x Hb x SaO2) + (k2 x PaO2); the normal oxygen extraction ratio O2ER is 0.2 to 0.3; each gram of Hb binds 1.39 mL of oxygen (the Hufner-constant variant this text uses); the inspired-oxygen table notes physiological shunt < 2% when breathing air.

sources.citation: Deranged Physiology. The concepts of venous admixture and shunt (CICM Primary Syllabus chapter F6(v)/(vi)), derangedphysiology.com.
sources.locator: The shunt (Berggren) equation Qs/Qt = (CcO2 - CaO2) / (CcO2 - CvO2). Venous admixture, as measured in normal subjects breathing room air, is usually about 3% of the cardiac output (value from Said & Banerjee 1963). Normal shunt fraction proper in healthy adults breathing room air is said to be close to 0% (probably 0.4-1%). Venous admixture integrates true shunt, V/Q scatter, Thebesian and bronchial venous drainage.

sources.citation: Physiology, Carbon Dioxide Response Curve. StatPearls (article text consulted in-session).
sources.locator: The carbon dioxide response curve is the nearly linear relationship between PaCO2 and minute ventilation: roughly 1 to 4 L/min increase in minute ventilation for each 1 mm Hg increase in PaCO2 (Miller's Anesthesia, as cited). Central chemoreceptors (medullary, H+-sensing) provide the majority of the response; peripheral chemoreceptors (carotid and aortic bodies) respond faster and also sense PaO2 and pH.

sources.citation: Hypercapnic ventilatory response - textbook summaries consulted in-session via ScienceDirect Topics (Kendig's Disorders of the Respiratory Tract in Children, 7th ed.; Chronic Respiratory Failure chapter).
sources.locator: VE = S x (PETCO2 - B). The carotid body provides about 20% to 30% of the total hypercapnic response, with a time constant of 10 to 30 seconds. The central chemoreceptor response accounts for about 70% to 80% of the total but is slower, with a time constant in the range of 60 to 150 seconds; steady-state ventilation has an apparently linear relationship to increasing PaCO2 (normal values for the hypercapnic ventilatory response slope range between 1 and 2 L/min per mm Hg of PCO2).

sources.citation: Apneic CO2-rise studies: (a) Stock MC et al. The carbon dioxide rate of rise in awake apneic humans. J Clin Anesth 1988 (abstract consulted in-session). (b) Carbon dioxide and cardiac output as major contributors to cerebral oxygenation during apnoeic oxygenation. Sci Rep 2024;14:3617 (PMC10864331).
sources.locator: (a) Awake breath-holding at functional residual capacity: PaCO2 rise about 7 mm Hg in the first 10 s and 2 mm Hg in the next 10 s (vascular equilibration), then about 6 mm Hg/min thereafter. (b) Apnoeic oxygenation under anaesthesia with high-flow nasal oxygen (which itself provides ventilatory exchange): mean PaCO2 rise 2.1 mm Hg/min over 15 min. The sustained unassisted rise therefore spans roughly 2-6 mm Hg/min across the consulted reports.

sources.citation: Phillips BP. Oxygen Transport: A Clinical Review. Boston Medical Center / Boston University School of Medicine, Critical Care Medicine teaching deck (consulted in-session).
sources.locator: DO2 = CO x CaO2 x 10, with CaO2 = (1.34 x Hb x SaO2) + (0.003 x PaO2); normal range (CO) for DO2: 800-1,000 mL/min; normal range (CI): 520-720 mL/min/m2; normal extraction ratio 22-32%; normal VO2 (indexed) 110-160 mL/min/m2.

sources.citation: Mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration - reference-range corpus consulted in-session (Wikipedia 'Mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration' and standard laboratory references).
sources.locator: MCHC reference range 32 to 36 g/dL (320 to 360 g/L). MCHC = hemoglobin / hematocrit; equivalently hemoglobin (g/dL) = MCHC x hematocrit (as a fraction). The Hgb/Hct ratio in healthy blood is close to 0.33.

sources.citation: Baynes JW, Dominiczak MH. Medical Biochemistry (oxygen-transport chapter; Student Consult text consulted in-session). Ferrell JE Jr. What is cooperativity? J Biol 2009;8:53.
sources.locator: Hill equation for hemoglobin saturation: Y = pO2^n / (P50^n + pO2^n). The normal value for adult Hb is n = 2.7 (Baynes); Ferrell: hemoglobin's binding 'is in fact fit by a Hill equation with a Hill coefficient of approximately 2.7'. Hb P50 = 27 +/- 2 mm Hg (Baynes); the commonly tabulated point value for a healthy person is 26.6 mm Hg.

sources.citation: Alveolar Minute Volume - reference table and worked examples (cal67 reference corpus, consulted in-session).
sources.locator: Alveolar minute volume (alveolar ventilation) = (tidal volume - dead space volume) x respiratory rate. Typical resting adult values: tidal volume 400-600 mL; respiratory rate 12-20 breaths/min; alveolar minute volume 4-6 L/min. Worked example: VT 500 mL, VD 150 mL, RR 12 gives (500 - 150) x 12 = 4.2 L/min.

sources.citation: Minute Ventilation - reference text (pulmolearn calculator reference, consulted in-session).
sources.locator: Minute ventilation VE = respiratory rate x tidal volume. Resting adult: about 5-8 L/min is the common resting range. Worked example: RR 12 breaths/min and VT 500 mL gives VE = 6 L/min.

sources.citation: Brandis K. Acid-Base Physiology (online text; Henderson-Hasselbalch relation and the respiratory compensation rules, consulted in-session).
sources.locator: Henderson-Hasselbalch: pH = pKa + log([HCO3-] / (0.03 x pCO2)), pKa 6.1. Rule 1, acute respiratory acidosis: [HCO3-] rises by 1 mmol/L for every 10 mmHg increase in pCO2 above its reference value of 40 mmHg (the increase is buffering only; there is no time for a renal response). Rule 3, acute respiratory alkalosis: [HCO3-] decreases by 2 mmol/L for every 10 mmHg decrease in pCO2 below 40 mmHg.

sources.citation: Arterial Oxygen Content - formula and reference table (cal67 reference corpus, consulted in-session).
sources.locator: CaO2 = (Hb x 1.34 x SaO2) + (PaO2 x 0.003), CaO2 in mL O2/dL blood. Reference table: CaO2 17-20 mL O2/dL blood; SaO2 95-100%; 1.34 is Hufner's constant (mL O2/g Hb; some sources use 1.36 or 1.39); 0.003 is the solubility coefficient of oxygen in plasma (mL O2/dL blood/mmHg).

sources.citation: Weil JV, Byrne-Quinn E, Sodal IE, Friesen WO, Underhill B, Filley GF, Grover RF. Hypoxic ventilatory drive in normal man. J Clin Invest 1970;49(6):1061-1072 (PMID 5422012).
sources.locator: Isocapnic VE-PAO2 curves are hyperbolic: falling PAO2 produces only slight rises in VE until a critical PAO2 range of 50-60 mm Hg is reached, below which VE rises steeply, the slope approaching infinity at a tension of 30-40 mm Hg. Quantitation by the hyperbolic function VE = VE0 + A / (PAO2 - 32): the constant 32 is the fitted asymptote. In 10 normal subjects at resting PACO2, A = 180.2 +/- 14.5 (SEM); when PACO2 was adjusted 5 mm Hg above and below control in six subjects, A = 453.4 +/- 103 and 30.2 +/- 6.8 respectively (the hypoxia-CO2 interaction in the paper's own numbers). Ventilatory adjustment to a PAO2 change is complete in 18-23 s. The paper also reports ventilation as a linear function of arterial oxygen saturation/content in four subjects - noted, not used: this engine's cited sensor quantity is PaO2 (S69).

sources.accessed: 2026-11-06, consulted in-session (textbook chapter reproduction read in-session)
sources.citation: Control of Breathing I: Chemical Mechanisms - textbook chapter on the chemical control of ventilation (consulted in-session via its web reproduction).
sources.locator: Peripheral chemoreceptors (carotid and aortic bodies) respond to decreased PO2 (not blood O2 content), increased PCO2 and [H+]; they are entirely responsible for the ventilatory response to hypoxia. At constant PACO2 there is little increase in ventilation until PAO2 falls below approximately 8 kPa (about 60 mm Hg). Reducing PAO2 steepens the slope of the CO2-ventilation relationship, and the effect of reducing PAO2 is potentiated if PACO2 is raised - 'a synergistic (more than additive) relationship between the effects of PAO2 and PACO2'. Central chemoreceptors account for about 80% of the CO2 response in humans.

sources.citation: Perioperative Optimization of Oxygen Delivery - review of oxygen-transport physiology and critical oxygen delivery (consulted in-session).
sources.locator: Under physiological conditions VO2 is independent of DO2: as DO2 falls the body maintains VO2 by increasing oxygen extraction and/or by increasing cardiac output. In the presence of a marked reduction of DO2 the extraction compensation is no longer sufficient, VO2 decreases in proportion to DO2, and the level below which this dependence appears is the critical oxygen delivery (DO2crit); below it the anaerobic pathway is used and lactic acid forms (tissue oxygen debt). Resting VO2 is 250-300 mL/min.

sources.citation: Oxygen delivery and consumption - Final FRCA revision corpus (consulted in-session).
sources.locator: Critical DO2 is the point below which VO2 becomes dependent on DO2, leading to anaerobic metabolism; its approximate value is about 300 mL/min in adults. Oxygen debt is the accumulated oxygen deficit during hypoxia, repaid during recovery. DO2 falls with low cardiac output, anaemia, or hypoxaemia; compensation for anaemia-class delivery falls is increased cardiac output and extraction.

sources.citation: Imai K et al. A New Look on the Position of the Oxygen Equilibrium Curve of Human Adult Hemoglobin at Rest and during Exercise with Special Reference to the Effectiveness of the Bohr Shift. Zoological Science 2001;18(7):905-918 (doi:10.2108/zsj.18.905).
sources.locator: Introduction: 'The magnitude of the Bohr effect is given by the change in log P50 (P50 is the O2 pressure at which Hb is 50% saturated with O2) per unit change in pH and is expressed as delta log P50 / delta pH (the Bohr coefficient). Under the physiological conditions, the Bohr coefficient for human adult Hb is -0.48.' The same paper's standard curve is whole blood at 37 C, pH 7.4, PCO2 40 torr, P50 26.7 torr. Consulted spread in-session: a review table of haemoglobins (Therapeutic Potential of Hemoglobin Derived from Arenicola marina, J Clin Med / PMC 2021) lists the human Hb Bohr coefficient as -0.48; a red-cell storage study (Front Physiol 2024) measures fresh red cells at -0.5 (per Hb tetramer); a comparative haemoglobin study (J Exp Biol 2013, citing Weber 1992) reports stripped human HbA at -0.56; a fish/human comparative review (J Appl Physiol 2017, citing Lapennas) spans air-breathing animals at -0.35 to -0.5. The whole-blood physiological value -0.48 is the one this engine takes (its Hill P50, S63, is a whole-blood value).

sources.citation: Brandis K. Acid-Base Physiology: Chapter 4.5 'Compensation', Chapter 6.5 'Respiratory Alkalosis - Compensation', and Chapter 9.3 'Bedside Rules' (the author's text, consulted via the Medicine LibreTexts reproduction and anaesthesiamcq.com).
sources.locator: Ch. 4.5: 'the average increase in plasma [HCO3-] in chronic respiratory acidosis is 4 mmol/l per 10 mmHg increase in PaCO2'; the renal response to a sustained PaCO2 rise 'is underway by 6 to 12 hours and usually takes a few days to reach its maximal value... the maximal effect is usually reached by 3 to 4 days'; the increased bicarbonate 'is usually NOT sufficient to return the pH to normal... typically, the pH will still be slightly acidotic'; the same chapter cites Martinu et al. (2003), who found an average rise of 5.1 mmol/l per 10 mmHg in stable chronic hypercapnic patients. Bedside Rule 2 (Ch. 9.3): 'For a chronic respiratory acidosis, the average change in [HCO3-] is 4 mmol/l for each 10 mmHg change in PaCO2 (from 40 mmHg)'; the renal compensation 'takes a few days to reach its maximal value'. Bedside Rule 4 / Ch. 6.5 (chronic respiratory alkalosis): the [HCO3-] falls 5 mmol/l for each 10 mmHg decrease in PaCO2; 'It takes 2 to 3 days to reach maximal renal compensation'; 'the limit of compensation is reached when the [HCO3-] falls to 12 to 15 mmol/l'. This is the same Brandis text as S66 (Henderson-Hasselbalch and the acute rules); S66 registered the acute rules only, and this entry registers the chronic rules consulted for Milestone 53.

sources.citation: eClinpath (Cornell University College of Veterinary Medicine) - 'Acid-base: Response to disturbances', acid-base module (consulted in full in-session).
sources.locator: On respiratory disturbances: 'The kidneys compensate for a chronic respiratory acid-base disturbance by increasing (respiratory acidosis) or decreasing (respiratory alkalosis) bicarbonate reabsorption. This response begins within hours but takes 3-5 days to have a full effect.' The page's expected-bicarbonate-change formulas use, for chronic respiratory acidosis, 0.35 mmol/L per mmHg PaCO2 change (HCO3 = 24 + 0.35 x (PaCO2 - 40), +/-2 mmol/L), and for chronic respiratory alkalosis 0.55 per mmHg - the consulted spread against S73's 0.4 / 0.5 bedside rules, disclosed in the chronic-slope parameters' notes. Consulted as the independent second source for the days-scale of full renal compensation in both directions and for the direction-split form of the relations.
